blocks.title: <ico-book></ico-book> WHAT IS SAID, WHAT IS MEANT
blocks.intro: Perfect grammar can still sound rude, and a polite phrase can hide a «no». This lesson is about how direct to be and how to hear what people mean. One thing first: styles vary by person and workplace, not by passport. You are learning signals to listen for, not rules about anyone.

vocab.sp: saying exactly what you think, without softening it
to give a certain impression: «He came across as rude.»
to understand what is meant but not said

vocab.en: to take something at face value
vocab.sp: to believe it means exactly what it says
to say no to an offer or invitation
to be busy and not available
to start doing something that was planned
thank you: I'll return the favor

blocks.note: How it works: flashcards , listening , compare , a dialogue with three difficult moments, gap-fill and memory. Press CHECK wherever you see it.

parts.html: 1 · THE DIRECTNESS SCALE — one request, five ways

items.en: Send me the file.
items.sp: 1 · An order. Fine in an emergency, or between close friends.

items.en: Can you send me the file?
items.sp: 2 · Direct, friendly.

items.en: Could you send me the file, please?
items.sp: 3 · The safe default at work.

items.en: Would you mind sending me the file?
items.sp: 4 · Polite: you are asking for a favor.

items.en: I was wondering if you could send me the file when you get a chance.
items.sp: 5 · Very soft: for someone senior, or someone you don't know.

parts.html: 2 · SOFTENERS AND DISTANCE — the past tense makes a request smaller

items.en: I was wondering if you had a minute.
items.sp: Past forms (was, had) for a present request: more distance, less pressure.

items.en: I wanted to ask about the deadline.
items.sp: «I wanted» is softer than «I want».

items.en: It might be an idea to check the numbers again.
items.sp: A suggestion dressed as a possibility.

items.en: Would it be possible to move the meeting?
items.sp: You ask about the possibility, not about the person.

parts.html: 3 · UNDERSTATEMENT — what these phrases often mean

items.en: That's an interesting idea.
items.sp: Often: I'm not convinced.

items.en: I'll bear it in mind.
items.sp: Often: I heard you, and I probably won't do it.

items.en: It's not bad at all.
items.sp: Often: it's good.

items.en: With respect, I see it differently.
items.sp: Always: I'm about to disagree.

parts.body: «Often» is the important word. Some people say «interesting» and mean interesting. Tone, the face and what comes next tell you which one it is. If you can't tell, go to step 5.

parts.html: 4 · FIVE WAYS TO SAY NO — without the word «no»

items.en: I'd love to, but I'm tied up on Friday.
items.sp: Warm feeling + reason.

items.en: I'm not sure that's going to work.
items.sp: Doubt instead of refusal.

items.en: That might be difficult.
items.sp: Usually a clear no.

items.en: Let me get back to you.
items.sp: Not now. Sometimes a real «later», sometimes a soft no.

items.en: I'm going to have to pass this time.
items.sp: A no that leaves the door open.

parts.html: 5 · WHEN IN DOUBT, CHECK — asking is not rude; guessing is risky

items.en: Just so I'm clear, is that a yes?
items.sp: The friendliest way to turn a hint into an answer.

items.en: So, to confirm: you'd like me to go ahead?
items.sp: You say what you understood and let them correct you.

parts.html: SPANISH TRAP — amable en español, una orden en inglés

items.en: Could I get a coffee, please?
items.sp: «Dame un café» suena amable en español. Give me a coffee suena a orden.

items.en: Thanks so much. I really appreciate it.
items.sp: El inglés espera más please y thank you que el español, incluso entre colegas.

items.en: You might want to check the date.
items.sp: You must check como consejo suena a orden. Para aconsejar: you should, you might want to.

items.en: I'd like the report by Friday.
items.sp: «Quiero» = I'd like. I want suena a exigencia.

parts.body: Give me a coffee. → Could I get a coffee, please? · You must call him. → You might want to call him. · I want the report. → I'd like the report.

blocks.title: <ico-star></ico-star> LOST IN TRANSLATION
blocks.intro:
It's the monthly World Panel. A listener has sent in a business idea, and four guests review it on air. All four dislike it. Only one says so. Roz gives you one job: count the real noes.

WORDS OF THE DAY (they must appear in your writing): blunt = saying exactly what you think · read between the lines · come across as.

cast.sp: hosts, and checks what people mean
the panel: from blunt to very indirect

blocks.title: AUDIO 1 · THE PANEL
blocks.desc: The idea: a café where you pay for the time you stay, not for what you drink. Four guests give their opinion. Listen for what each one says, and for what each one means.

questions.q: How many of the four guests would invest in the café?
What does Sam's "I'll bear it in mind" signal here?
Whose feedback could the listener most easily mistake for approval?
Which phrase does Nora use to find out what they really think?

speaking.prompt: Give the listener your own feedback on the café idea in three sentences: honest, but not blunt. Finish with one useful suggestion.
speaking.starter: There's a lot I like about… I was wondering if… It might be an idea to…

transcript.html: Welcome to the World Panel. Every month, a listener sends us a business idea, and four guests tell us what they think. Tonight's idea: a café where you pay for the time you stay, not for what you drink. Five dollars an hour, coffee included. Max, you run a store. Would you invest?
No. I'll be direct: the numbers don't work. One customer with a laptop takes a table for four hours and pays twenty dollars. You'd lose money on every table. I wouldn't put a cent into it.
Well, it's certainly an interesting idea. I was wondering whether the price had been tested with real customers. It might be an idea to try it for a month before signing a lease.
It's not bad at all, as a concept. I'm just not sure it's going to work in this city, at this moment. With a few changes, who knows?
And Sam, you opened a bakery from nothing.
It's very brave. Very original. I'd say the author should definitely keep thinking about it. I'll bear it in mind if I ever expand.
Hmm. Let me check something, because our listener is hearing "interesting," "not bad," and "brave." Just so I'm clear: would any of you put your own money into this café? Kit?

So that's four noes, and only Max said the word. To our listener: read between the lines. Kit gave you the most useful advice tonight, and she never said "no" at all. Test the price first. We'll be right back.

blocks.title: THE ORDER vs THE REQUEST
blocks.intro: Both get you the file. Think about how each one lands on the person who reads it.

pair.b: Could you send me the file when you get a chance?

items.q: Which one reads as an order, even from a friendly person?
What does "when you get a chance" add?
options: Room: there is no pressure on time

items.q: You are writing to a colleague you hardly know. Which is safest?
options: I was wondering if you could send me the file.

items.q: You need it urgently, and you still want to be polite. Which one?
options: Could you send me the file by three? Sorry for the rush.
You must send it by three.

items.q: Which is advice, not an order?
options: You must back up that file.
You might want to back up that file.

blocks.title: THREE DIFFICULT MOMENTS
blocks.intro: After the show: you turn down an invitation (you can't go on Friday), give honest feedback (you think Roz's new opening is too long), and ask a favor. Pick the reply that is honest and keeps the relationship.

lines.html: A few of us are going for dinner after the show on Friday. You should come!

options: I'd love to, but I'm tied up on Friday. Next time, definitely.
I can't. I have something better to do.

lines.html: Oh, that's a pity. Are you sure?

options: I'm afraid so. But thanks for asking. I really appreciate it.

lines.html: So, what did you think of my new opening for the show? Be honest.

options: It's perfect. Don't change a thing.
There's a lot I like. I was wondering if the first minute might be a little long.

lines.html: Too long? Hmm. What would you do?

options: It might be an idea to start with the music and cut the first two lines.
You must cut the first two lines.
I don't know. It's your job, not mine.

lines.html: You look worried. Is everything okay?

options: I wanted to ask you a favor. Would you mind looking at my script when you get a chance?
I want you to check my script today.

lines.html: Of course. Is tomorrow morning all right?

options: That would be great. Thanks so much. I owe you one.

blocks.title: AUDIO 2 · THE EMAIL
blocks.desc: Theo reads a message from a listener who offended his new manager with an email in which every word was correct. Find the three lines that did the damage.

questions.q: What was the problem with the listener's email?
options: It was full of grammar mistakes
It was correct, but it read like a list of orders

questions.q: What does Theo suggest in place of "You must check the numbers"?
options: You might want to check the numbers.
You have to check the numbers.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the three problem lines?
options: Send me the sales report today.
I want an answer before five.

questions.q: What does Theo mean by "Same message, different music"?
options: The content was fine; the tone was the problem
The listener should have called instead

speaking.prompt: Say the listener's email again, politely: a greeting, the request, the suggestion, the deadline and a thank-you.
speaking.starter: Hi Dana, could you… You might want to… I'd appreciate… Thanks so much.

transcript.html: Now, a letter. It comes from a listener who has started a new job, and he writes: "Theo, I think I offended my new manager, and I don't know how. This is the email I sent her." Here it is. "Hello Dana. Send me the sales report today. You must check the numbers before, because last time there were errors. I want an answer before five. Regards."

He says every word is correct. And it is. So where's the problem? Three lines. "Send me the report" is an order. Try "Could you send me the report?" "You must check" sounds like a boss talking down. Try "You might want to check." And "I want an answer" is a demand. "I'd appreciate an answer" gets the same result.
Oh, and not one "please" or "thank you" in four lines. At his last office, he tells me, that was perfectly friendly. At this one, it isn't. Same message, different music.

blocks.title: <ico-pen></ico-pen> SAY NO, KEEP THE FRIEND
blocks.intro: A colleague asks you to cover their shift on Saturday, or to finish their report, or to lend them money: you choose. You can't, or you don't want to. Write your reply (about 80 words).
checklist: One softener (I'd love to, but… / I'm afraid… / I'm not sure that's going to work)
One honest reason, in one sentence
The words of the day: blunt, read between the lines, come across as
blocks.placeholder: Hi …, thanks for thinking of me.
blocks.example: Hi name, thanks for -ing form. I'd love to help, but softener + what you can't do. your reason, one sentence. I don't want to come across as adjective, so what you want them to understand. What I can do is your alternative. Would that verb?
blocks.hw: Write your reply, then record yourself saying it as you would face to face: warm voice, no hurry. Send me the text and the audio on WhatsApp.

rubric.d: About 80 words: the colleague understands that the answer is no, why, and what you can offer.
No «no», one softener, one reason and one alternative; nothing in it reads as an order or an excuse.
The reader does not have to guess. Polite and clear at the same time.
